newsitem.title: USA: Childhood vaccinations exceed government's goals.
newsitem.headline: Childhood vaccinations exceed government's goals.

text.p: More than 90 percent of the nation's infants have received the recommended vaccines against measles, polio, tetanus and diphtheria, exceeding the government's childhood vaccination goals, health officials said on Wednesday.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said 95 percent of 2-year-olds received the recommended three doses of a diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis vaccine; and 92 percent had received three doses of vaccine against Haemophilus influenzae type B, a cause of spinal meningitis.
The health agency's National Immunisation Survey also found that 91 percent of infants had received a measles vaccination and the recommended three doses of polio vaccine.

Officials said the figures exceeded the goals established under a childhood immunisation effort launched by President Bill Clinton in 1993. However, the CDC said nearly a million 2-year-olds are still not fully immunised.
Researchers said there were no reported cases of tetanus among children younger than 15 in 1996, no cases of polio due to wild polio virus and only four cases of diphtheria.
The CDC said there were 165 cases of Haemophilus influenzae invasive disease among children under 5 years, 196 cases of rubella (German measles) and 443 cases of measles.

"The few hundred cases of vaccine-preventable diseases that occurred in 1996 stand in marked contrast to the thousands of cases that occurred annually in the five years before our initiative began," CDC Director Dr. David Satcher said in a statement.

The CDC recommends childhood vaccinations to prevent ten infectious diseases: polio, measles, diphtheria, mumps, pertussis (whooping cough), rubella, tetanus, Haemophilus influenzae type b, varicella (chicken pox), and hepatitis-B.
